drills.q: A test suite has 95% line coverage on a critical module, and a bug still reached production. What does this suggest, and what's your next diagnostic step?
drills.a: High line coverage only confirms lines executed, not that any assertion would catch them being wrong. Run mutation testing scoped to that module to find surviving mutants -- concrete evidence of exactly which logic no test actually verifies.

drills.q: Tests pass individually but fail intermittently depending on execution order. What's the likely cause?
drills.a: A session- or module-scoped fixture holds mutable state that one test modifies, silently affecting a later test. Fix: narrow the fixture to function scope if isolation is needed, or explicitly reset the shared state at the start of each test using it.

drills.q: A serialization function passes all example-based tests for months, then fails on a specific real-world unicode input in production. Diagnose and propose a fix.
drills.a: Example-based tests only check inputs an engineer thought to write, systematically under-sampling the true input space (unusual unicode, boundary lengths, nesting). Fix: add a Hypothesis round-trip property test (decode(encode(x))==x) over the actual input domain, letting generated and auto-shrunk examples surface the missed case class.

drills.q: If a mutant is killed by your test suite, does that guarantee the corresponding code is bug-free?
drills.a: No -- it only proves sensitivity to that one specific mechanical mutation (e.g. one operator swap). It says nothing about a different kind of bug in the same line that doesn't correspond to any mutation in the catalog, or a bug from interaction with other code.

drills.q: Design a test-quality improvement plan for a payments module with 90% coverage and two recent production incidents.
drills.a: First, run mutation testing scoped to the module to get a ranked list of surviving mutants -- targeted, evidence-based gap identification. Second, for revealed weak spots, decide Hypothesis property tests (numerical invariants like transaction reconciliation) vs added parametrize cases (specific boundary/rounding edge cases) as appropriate. Third, add tests, then re-run mutation testing to verify previously-surviving mutants are now killed.

drills.q: A full mutation-testing pass on your payments module takes 6 hours. How do you make this a sustainable ongoing practice?
drills.a: Don't run the full pass on every commit -- schedule it periodically (monthly, or before major releases of that module) as a diagnostic/validation tool. Add the newly-identified test cases to the fast, always-on test suite so their value is captured continuously, even though the mutation-testing verification itself stays periodic.

drills.q: After shipping a performance-optimized function validated with a differential Hypothesis property against the old reference implementation, should you delete the reference implementation and its test?
drills.a: Not necessarily -- keep the reference implementation as a clearly-marked test-only artifact so the differential test continues providing value on every future change to the optimized version. Deleting it removes the ability to keep verifying 'still behaves the same as the known-correct-but-slow version' going forward.

drills.q: How would you decide whether a specific module in your codebase actually warrants investing in mutation testing, versus relying on example-based tests and monitoring/rollback?
drills.a: Weigh the module's blast radius if a subtle bug slips through, the cost/reversibility of an incident there (quickly rolled back with minimal harm, or lasting damage before detection), and its historical incident rate. High blast radius + low reversibility + a track record of incidents is a strong candidate; scoring low on all three is a weak candidate not worth the computational and triage cost.
